item.title: Kibinago Sashimi & Island Seafood — Guide
item.description: Kagoshima’s warm southern seas and many islands make it a superb seafood destination, and one of its most distinctive local delicacies is kibinago — the silver-stripe round herring, a tiny, slender, silvery fish. Caught in local waters, these delicate little fish are most beautifully served as sashimi: gutted, filleted and arranged by hand in a striking chrysanthemum-flower or fan pattern on the plate, their silver-and-blue skin gleaming. They’re eaten dipped not in ordinary soy sauce but in ‘sumiso’ — a sweet-tangy vinegared miso — which perfectly complements their light, delicate flavour.

item.title: Katsuura Morning Market & Sashimi Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The fishing town of Katsuura on the Boso coast is a paradise for seafood lovers, home to one of Japan’s three great morning markets — a tradition running for over 400 years. Each morning, stalls along the old streets brim with the night’s catch, vegetables and pickles, and nearby diners serve glistening sashimi rice bowls and set meals built around the day’s freshest fish straight off the boats. Katsuura is also the surprising birthplace of fiery Katsuura tantanmen, a local spicy ramen.

item.title: Chiba Food Guide: Unagi, Sashimi, Peanuts & Pacific Seafood
item.description: Chiba Prefecture sits on the Pacific and Tokyo Bay, and its food culture reflects that position directly. The prefecture produces over 80 percent of Japan’s peanuts, operates Japan’s largest fishing port at Choshi, and hosts one of the oldest unagi-dining traditions in the country along the approach road to Naritasan Temple. For overseas visitors willing to venture beyond Narita Airport’s restaurants and the Disney Resort food courts, Chiba offers some of the most distinctive and affordable culinary experiences in the entire Kanto region.
